The paper package from the previous chapter is now contained. Its manuscript
has been preserved, its code has run in a bounded environment, its model and
dependency identities are known, and its release status has not been inferred
from local success. One test passes. The proposed adapter produces the expected
output on the example supplied by the authors.

What, exactly, did the book learn?

The shortest answer is tempting: the paper works. That sentence is also
wrong. A passing example may show that one command produced one expected
result in one observed environment. It may support a claim about the example,
the command, or the implementation under that configuration. It does not by
itself show that the paper's mechanism caused the result, that the result
generalizes, that the evaluator measured the right property, that the adapter
is safe, that the source's interpretation is correct, or that any architectural
claim in this book should become more confident.

The distinction is easy to state and hard to preserve. People naturally read
evidence outward. A test result becomes evidence for the implementation, then
for the method, then for the design principle, then for the larger system. A
paper citation lends authority to the paragraph around it. A formal proof
makes nearby empirical language feel more certain. A sophisticated reviewer
makes the conclusion look independently checked. An activation plot makes an
internal mechanism seem visible. Each step may be reasonable, but none follows
automatically from the previous one.

This chapter develops the stack's answer: evidence must move through stable
claim identities, declared roles, bounded inferences, and review paths that
remain honest about dependence and evaluator limits. The purpose is not to
turn judgment into a database operation. It is to prevent a useful artifact
from speaking for claims it never tested.

The security layer controlled who could read, run, and release the package.
The evidence layer controls what conclusions may survive from what happened.
That control is just as important. A perfectly isolated experiment can still
measure the wrong construct, compare against a weak baseline, omit failed
cases, or persuade a reviewer who lacks the information needed to challenge
it.

## A Passing Test Is Not a General Verdict

Begin with three different objects. The first is a claim: a proposition with
words, scope, and conditions under which it could be wrong. The second is an
evidence artifact: a source passage, test result, proof object, evaluation
transcript, model-internal observation, or review record. The third is the
world: the implementation and environment whose behavior matters.

Those objects can disagree. A claim can be precise while its evidence is weak.
An artifact can be authentic while the represented event is misunderstood. A
proof can be valid for a finite model while the deployed system violates the
model's assumptions. A benchmark can be reproduced while measuring a poor
proxy. A runtime can behave correctly while the claim describing it is too
broad. Good evidence discipline begins by refusing to collapse the three.

For the incoming adapter, the passing example has a narrow identity. It names
the exact source commit, model configuration, command, fixture, environment,
expected output, observed output, and time. It can support a sentence such as:
*under this recorded configuration, the example completed and matched its
declared expected result*. Even this sentence should preserve the command log,
failures, and environmental assumptions that make it inspectable.

The artifact cannot support *the method is generally effective* without a
workload and comparator. It cannot support *the mechanism caused the gain*
without interventions that distinguish the proposed mechanism from plausible
alternatives. It cannot support *the adapter is safe* without a threat model,
adversarial controls, and effect observations. It cannot support *the ASI Stack
is validated* because one component-level run is not an end-to-end test of the
architecture.

This narrowing is not pedantry. It protects useful evidence. When a broad
claim later fails, the exact passing observation can remain true. When a
dependency changes, the result can expire without erasing its history. When a
better evaluator reveals that the measured property was wrong, the book can
revise the interpretation while retaining the original artifact. Evidence
becomes more reusable when its maximum inference is explicit.

The same rule applies to negative results. Suppose the adapter fails on a
second task. The failure should be recorded before anyone explains it away.
But *this run failed* is not identical to *the implementation is incapable*,
and neither is identical to *the architecture is refuted*. A missing
dependency, weak training setup, inadequate evaluator, or malformed task can
narrow what the failure tests. Competence review may change the maximum
inference without rewriting the raw outcome.

This distinction matters in a living book because prose can improve faster
than evidence. A revision may make an argument clearer, remove a weak analogy,
or connect two mechanisms more convincingly. Better writing is valuable, but
it is not a support transition. If exposition and evidence are allowed to move
together by mood, the most polished chapter will gradually sound the most
proven.

## Claims Need Stable Identities

A claim is not merely a sentence at a page location. It is an object that
persists while wording, scope, and evidence change. Its record needs at least a
stable identity, current text, claim kind, scope, support state, evidence
references, limitations, defeaters, descendants, and history.

Stable identity solves a practical problem. The same sentence can mean
different things under different quantifiers. “The adapter improves source
routing” might refer to one fixture, one family of papers, the current
repository, or technical writing in general. An evaluation over ten curated
examples may be relevant to the first two and silent about the others. If the
claim has no identity beyond its prose, evidence can attach to the broadest
reading after the fact.

The stack therefore separates a core architectural claim from narrower
subclaims. A core might say that consequential evidence should move through a
versioned claim ledger. Subclaims can address whether a schema captures the
needed fields, whether a validator rejects identity substitution, whether a
review protocol finds an omitted failure, or whether the full system improves
calibration on natural work. Those claims share a topic but not a support
state.

This is why support does not inherit freely. A successful fixture for the
record shape does not promote the natural-work claim. A useful oversight
protocol does not establish the competence of every reviewer. A causal
intervention on one checkpoint does not establish a universal mechanism. A
parent chapter does not inherit the proof or experiment of a technical child,
and a child does not inherit the rhetorical importance of its parent.

Stable identities also make revision safer. When a claim is narrowed, the
ledger can retain the previous wording, the reason for narrowing, and the
evidence that survives. When two claims are discovered to be different, they
can split without pretending that all prior evidence applies equally. When a
claim is deprecated, dependent conclusions can be located and re-examined.

The alternative is confidence by adjacency. A citation placed near three
sentences appears to support all three. A proof badge near a chapter title
colors the whole chapter. A benchmark table makes the surrounding mechanism
sound measured. Stable claim identity turns adjacency back into an explicit
mapping question: which artifact supports which proposition, in which role,
under which limit?

## Support States Are Not a Confidence Score

The book uses support states, but they should not be read as one universal
ladder from weak to strong. Source-derived, mechanized, prototype-backed,
synthetic-test-backed, empirical-test-backed, and external-literature-backed
evidence answer different questions.

A source note can establish what another author argued or measured. It does
not reproduce the result locally. A proof can establish a theorem inside its
formal assumptions. It does not show that the assumptions describe the
runtime. A synthetic fixture can test a transition or rejection path exactly.
It may have little transfer to natural work. An empirical result can measure a
real workload while suffering from poor construct validity or dependence. An
external replication can add independence while testing a narrower variant.

No fixed arithmetic makes one category dominate all others. The relevant
question depends on the claim. If the claim concerns a finite state-machine
invariant, a proof may be decisive within that scope. If it concerns operator
fatigue, a formal theorem over authored fields cannot replace human evidence.
If it concerns source lineage, an exact passage may matter more than a local
simulation. If it concerns deployment safety, no single evidence role is
likely to be sufficient.

The public support state is therefore a summary. Behind it sits an evidence
cell that keeps quality dimensions separate: independence, reproducibility,
recency, coverage, adversarial strength, validity, artifact access, and
transfer distance. A result can be reproducible but dependent, adversarial but
poorly targeted, current but inaccessible, or broad but weakly causal.
Allowing one dimension to compensate automatically for another would hide the
reason a reviewer should trust or distrust the result.

The evidence cell also retains negative and null evidence. A campaign that
finds no advantage against a strong baseline can leave the claim unchanged,
narrow it, or refute a precise subclaim. An inconclusive attempt can establish
that the instrument was inadequate. A failure to reproduce can reveal a
configuration dependency without resolving which implementation is correct.
These are not embarrassing leftovers. They are part of the denominator that
makes future positive results interpretable.

## An Evidence Transition Is a Bounded Argument

Support changes through a transition rather than through an edit. The
transition names the claim before and after, the proposed support movement,
the artifacts being used, their evidence roles, the consumer, the reviewer,
the maximum inference, the limitations, the negative evidence, the dissent,
the expiry conditions, and the dependent claims that may need review.

This is not an attempt to automate epistemology. The transition is a compact
argument with enough structure to be challenged. Its fields prevent common
omissions, but a shape-valid record can still contain false statements, a weak
construct, or a captured reviewer. The record earns no authority merely by
existing.

The transition for the paper's passing example might request movement for one
implementation subclaim from argument to synthetic-test-backed. The reviewer
checks that the fixture was prospective rather than selected after the result,
that the environment and expected output are bound, that failed cases remain
visible, that the evaluator did not share the implementation defect being
tested, and that the resulting sentence stays inside the observation.

The transition should be rejected if the requested claim is broader than the
artifact. It should also be rejected if the evidence is authentic but
inapplicable, if the evaluator cannot inspect the relevant property, if a
material dependency is stale, or if the proposal attempts to move a parent or
neighbor claim. Rejection preserves the artifact. It says only that the
requested inference did not pass.

Downward movement needs equal discipline. A contradiction, failed proof,
invalidated dataset, benchmark contamination, implementation failure, or new
counterexample can narrow, downgrade, refute, deprecate, or expire a claim.
The transition records which conclusion changed and which did not. This avoids
two opposite errors: hiding negative evidence to protect the architecture, and
letting an incompetent attempt refute an idea it never actually tested.

Every accepted transition ends with a bounded handoff. The claim ledger owns
the support record. It does not authorize deployment, training, publication,
or tool use. Those decisions may consume the support state, but they remain
separate acts with their own owners.

## Oversight Begins Where the Evaluator Is Weaker

Evidence discipline becomes difficult when the system being evaluated can
produce work that no single reviewer can fully reconstruct. A model may search
more alternatives, read more context, write more code, or exploit a domain
specialism that exceeds the evaluator's immediate capacity. Scalable oversight
asks whether decomposition, consultation, debate, critics, audits, tools, and
selective escalation can help limited supervisors evaluate stronger systems.

The word *scalable* does not mean that adding reviewers automatically solves
the problem. It means that review protocols themselves become evaluated
components. A protocol needs a task and authority scope, a supervisor
capability envelope, the evidence available to each role, a comparison
baseline, known dependencies, an outcome audit where possible, a residual
owner, a permitted consumer, and an escalation route.

Consider the adapter's proposed integration. A strong model argues that the
passing example and clean static checks justify adoption. A smaller critic is
asked to challenge it. A human reviewer chooses between them. This sounds like
three layers of oversight, but the arrangement may be weaker than it appears.
The critic might see only the model's summary rather than the raw logs. Both
models may share the same base family and retrieval corpus. The human may lack
time to inspect the omitted cases. The test harness may have been written by
the same process that wrote the adapter.

A useful oversight record exposes those dependencies. It names what each role
could observe, what it could not observe, which incentives and tools it shared,
and what outcome could later reveal whether the review was right. The protocol
is compared with a competent simpler baseline, such as one informed human
reviewing the complete frozen report without model advocacy.

The protocol can then earn a narrow result. Perhaps the critic notices that
the passing example used a source category excluded from the book's actual
intake path. An independent replay confirms the mismatch. The protocol has
helped find a real defect. It has not proved that debate is generally reliable,
that the critic is independent, or that the adapter should be adopted. The
evidence system can record the finding; the authority owner can keep the
change quarantined.

Where no admissible outcome exists, the honest state is unresolved. The system
may narrow the task, acquire better evidence, ask a qualified reviewer, hold
the decision, or accept an explicitly owned residual under existing authority.
It may not turn a long transcript or majority vote into truth by default.

## Independence Is a Dependency Graph

Review roles are often counted as if independence were a head count. A
proposer, critic, judge, and auditor look like four checks. If they share the
same model weights, prompts, retrieval source, benchmark leakage, reward
signal, tool defect, or organizational incentive, they may reproduce one
error four times.

Independence is better represented as a dependency graph. Nodes are people,
models, instruments, datasets, prompts, tools, and decision owners. Edges show
shared training, information, incentives, implementation, or authority. The
graph does not produce a binary certificate of independence. It tells the
reviewer which correlated failures still need a challenge.

For example, two model families may have different weights but share the same
evaluation dataset. Two human reviewers may be organizationally separate but
use the same summary dashboard. A deterministic test may be independent of a
model's persuasion but depend on a schema that omits the decisive property. An
external paper may be independent in authorship while using the same benchmark
and assumptions.

The response is not maximal diversity. Additional reviewers consume time,
money, privacy, and attention, and can create new persuasion surfaces. The goal
is targeted separation. A suspected parser defect calls for a separately
implemented parser or direct artifact inspection. A causal claim calls for an
intervention that breaks the proposed mechanism while preserving plausible
alternatives. A concern about benchmark leakage calls for a held-out or newly
constructed cohort. A high-consequence decision with no adequate evaluator may
call for refusal rather than another model vote.

Reviewer capacity also changes over time. Queue pressure, alarm fatigue,
automation bias, repeated approval, and persuasive presentation can degrade a
nominally capable supervisor. A receipt showing that a human clicked approve
does not establish that meaningful review occurred. The record should preserve
the decision window, evidence view, intervention path, workload, unresolved
conflicts, and whether a stop would have changed the system's behavior.

## White-Box Evidence Starts a New Challenge

Behavioral tests observe what a model did. White-box methods inspect internal
states: activations, probe outputs, sparse features, circuits, attribution
graphs, or the effects of interventions. These methods can reveal hypotheses
that behavior alone may miss. They also create a powerful temptation to treat
visibility as understanding.

Suppose an analysis finds an activation that rises on examples labeled
deceptive. The activation predicts the benchmark label, and suppressing it
reduces deceptive answers. It is natural to call the feature “deception” and
present the intervention as causal evidence. A matched control may reveal a
different explanation: the activation tracks discussion of hypothetical
agents across both deceptive and honest examples. Suppression reduces the
benchmark behavior because it suppresses the topic more broadly.

The original observation remains useful. The label and inference change. A
white-box evidence packet therefore preserves the exact model and checkpoint,
capture population, extraction method, hyperparameters, reconstruction error,
label author, positive and negative examples, alternative labels, predictive
performance, intervention semantics, side effects, stability, unexplained
residuals, and expiry.

The inference proceeds through a ladder. Capturing an internal state does not
make it meaningful. Extracting a feature does not make the feature natural or
unique. Assigning a label does not make it the model's own concept. Predicting
behavior does not show that the model uses the feature. An intervention that
changes behavior does not establish specificity, completeness, or safety. A
useful research intervention does not authorize an activation policy in
deployment.

Different methods ask different questions. A probe can show that information
is available to a chosen probe family while learning the task itself from weak
traces. A sparse dictionary can produce readable features while splitting,
merging, or changing them across checkpoints and corpora. A circuit analysis
can identify a sufficient path without proving that it is the only path. An
ablation can damage unrelated computation. Steering can improve the measured
behavior while moving the risk outside the evaluator's view.

Stronger evidence comes from distinct challenges. Does the hypothesis predict
held-out behavior beyond simple behavioral signals? Is the proposed component
necessary under one intervention? Is it sufficient in an appropriate context?
Are unrelated capabilities preserved? Does effect strength change coherently
with intervention dose? Do alternative methods and checkpoints recover a
compatible bounded story? Which behavior and computation remain unexplained?

Even a good answer earns only a scoped status. It may justify additional
scrutiny, a bounded causal claim, or a candidate monitor. The monitor or
steering rule is a new model component with false positives, false negatives,
latency, privacy exposure, side effects, fallback, rollback, and expiry. It
must be qualified separately against a strong behavioral baseline.

This is why white-box evidence belongs inside the broader evaluation-integrity
family while retaining its own technical owner. Behavioral discrepancies do
not identify internal causes. Internal observations do not establish
deception, sandbagging, or intent. The two evidence paths can constrain and
challenge one another without inheriting each other's conclusions.

## One Patch, Three Evidence Paths

Return to the paper-ingestion change. The adapter proposes a mapping from new
paper passages to existing chapter owners. Its authors claim that an internal
routing representation makes the mapping more consistent and cheaper to
review. The repository now has three evidence paths.

The first path is behavioral. A prospective fixture presents papers with known
ownership distinctions and records the adapter's mappings, abstentions,
errors, and costs against a simple rule-based baseline and a direct strong-model
baseline. The passing example establishes one observation. A broader claim
requires the complete denominator, failures, matched access, and a workload
that was not selected after seeing the adapter's strengths.

The second path is oversight. A critic receives the paper, the candidate
mapping, the owner definitions, and the same source boundaries as the
proposer. A human reviewer receives both arguments and the underlying passages.
An independent outcome check asks whether the accepted mapping preserves the
book's canonical ownership graph. The protocol records shared dependencies and
compares the assisted path with informed direct review.

The third path is internal. A probe or sparse feature appears to distinguish
mechanism-bearing passages from examples and background. The analysis records
the exact checkpoint, extraction method, label construction, reconstruction,
counterexamples, and stability. It tests whether the feature predicts held-out
ownership decisions beyond surface vocabulary and whether interventions alter
the target decision without damaging unrelated routing.

The three paths do not vote on one universal verdict. The behavioral path may
show that the adapter works on a bounded cohort. The oversight path may show
that assisted review finds a particular omission. The internal path may remain
predictive but not causal. The claim ledger can accept, reject, or defer
separate transitions for each proposition.

Suppose the behavioral fixture passes, the critic finds no new errors, and the
internal feature is unstable across a checkpoint update. The correct result is
not “two of three checks passed.” The implementation subclaim may gain bounded
synthetic support. The oversight protocol may record no demonstrated advantage
over direct review. The internal-mechanism claim may remain unsupported or
expire. The architecture-level claim remains at its prior state.

Now suppose a later outcome audit finds that the fixture omitted papers with
mixed normative and implementation content. That discovery can invalidate the
transition that depended on the cohort without erasing the exact examples that
did pass. Descendant claims and decisions are located through identity, not
through recollection. The adapter may return to quarantine, the test may be
revised prospectively, and the negative result remains part of the next
denominator.

This is the practical value of the machinery: not confidence, but controlled
revision. The system can learn without pretending that every artifact agrees,
and it can recover without deleting the history that explains why confidence
changed.

## Failure Cases

**Citation laundering.** A source is accurately cited but mapped to a broader
claim than the passage supports. The cure is claim-specific source mapping and
a visible limit, not more citations.

**Proof halo.** A theorem about a finite record lifecycle makes readers infer
that the recorded event is true or the deployed system is safe. The proof must
state its trusted inputs and maximum inference beside the theorem-bearing
claim.

**Fixture inflation.** A synthetic test of schema or transition behavior is
reported as evidence of natural-task utility. The claim identity and evidence
role must keep record behavior separate from world behavior.

**Result cherry-picking.** Passing cases are reported while failed, retried,
abstained, or excluded cases disappear. Complete denominators and immutable
raw outcomes prevent a cleaned summary from replacing the campaign.

**Parent promotion.** A narrow child claim gains evidence and the larger
chapter or architecture inherits the movement. Support transitions must name
their exact target and reject upward or lateral inheritance.

**Correlated oversight.** Several reviewers share the same blind spot and are
counted as independent agreement. Dependency disclosure and targeted
correlation challenges replace head count with a falsifiable review claim.

**Persuasion theater.** A fluent advocate convinces a weak judge without an
admissible outcome audit. High-risk results route to escalation or residual
custody rather than automatic admission.

**Coverage laundering.** Hard cases, abstentions, and unresolved disagreements
are removed from the reported score. Coverage, selective risk, queue effects,
and escalation outcomes remain beside accuracy.

**White-box semantic leap.** A readable feature receives an attractive label,
then prediction and intervention are treated as proof of a complete mechanism.
Alternative constructs, controls, side effects, method disagreement, and
unexplained residuals remain first-class evidence.

**Monitor self-certification.** A monitor or steering policy is trusted because
the interpretation that motivated it looked causal. The policy is treated as
a new component and tested separately for failure, gaming, collateral effects,
cost, rollback, and drift.

**Stale reuse.** An evidence receipt survives a changed model, task, prompt,
dataset, evaluator, protocol, or decision. Material-change triggers expire the
dependent inference and require re-admission.

**Authority laundering.** A support transition becomes permission to train,
deploy, publish, or use tools. The claim ledger can inform those owners but
cannot impersonate them.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest simpler baseline is not an unstructured conversation. It is a
small, append-only review record attached to a precise claim. The record names
the proposition, source or result, scope, reviewer, decision, limitation, and
date. A competent human reads the complete artifact, compares it with a
declared baseline, and updates the record. No elaborate support taxonomy,
delegated debate, dependency graph, or white-box packet is required unless it
changes the decision.

This baseline can be very strong. Many claims do not need a complex state
machine. A source attribution may need only an exact passage and an honest
summary. A deterministic regression may need a pinned command and result. A
small, transparent code change may be easier to inspect directly than to route
through multiple AI reviewers. A behavioral test may dominate an expensive
interpretability analysis.

The stack should lose where that baseline preserves the same calibration,
challenge, revision, and recovery at lower cost. Complexity is justified only
when the simpler record predictably loses claim identity, dependence,
negative evidence, expiry, or consumer boundaries that matter to consequential
decisions.

This comparison prevents governance from becoming self-validating. The
question is not whether a richer ledger can represent more information. It is
whether the additional structure finds consequential errors, improves
calibration, preserves disagreement, reduces unsafe inference, or makes
revision and recovery materially better after reviewer time and system cost
are included.

## What the Current Evidence Can Establish

The live technical book contains formal models, schemas, fixtures, source
notes, and bounded campaigns related to claim transitions, oversight, and
white-box evidence. Those artifacts establish narrow properties about the
records the repository actually checks. They can show, for example, that a
finite transition rejects identity substitution, that a bounded oversight
route refuses an incomplete handoff, or that an internal-evidence packet
preserves declared fields and non-authority boundaries.

They do not establish that the fields are true, that a reviewer is competent,
that a model's trace is faithful, that a probe has found a genuine semantic
feature, that an intervention is safe, that scalable oversight works on
superhuman tasks, or that the full evidence system improves natural work.
Source-reported interpretability and oversight results remain evidence about
their own studies, not local reproduction or universal validation.

The three routed chapter cores remain at argument support. Their formal and
executable artifacts belong to narrower subclaims and record-lifecycle
properties. This Human Reader synthesis does not combine those narrower
results into a stronger conclusion. It explains why the interfaces are
needed and what experiments would justify keeping them.

## From Minimum Implementation to a Mature Evidence System

The minimum viable implementation is small. Give every material claim a stable
identity, current wording, scope, support state, evidence references,
limitations, and immutable transition history. Require every proposed movement
to name its target, artifact role, maximum inference, reviewer, negative
evidence, and expiry. Reject movement to parents or neighbors. Keep deployment
and publication authority elsewhere.

Add scalable oversight only where the evaluator gap matters. The first useful
protocol records the task, risk, evidence views, role dependencies, direct
review baseline, outcome-audit status, permitted consumer, abstention or
residual, and escalation owner. High-risk results without adequate outcome
evidence do not become training labels, claim transitions, or release inputs.

Add white-box evidence only where internal access might change a decision. The
first packet binds the model, checkpoint, capture, extraction assumptions,
label provenance, predictive test, intervention, controls, side effects,
stability, residual, and maximum inference. A readable visualization is not a
completed packet. A causal-bounded result is not a release decision.

A mature system would maintain a living claim graph. It would know which
sources, proofs, tests, evaluations, internal observations, and decisions
depend on each claim version. New evidence could strengthen one proposition,
narrow another, expire a third, and leave the parent unchanged. Contradictions
and null results would remain searchable. Dissent would be preserved rather
than averaged away.

Oversight would become an adaptive but governed service. Review protocols
would be selected by risk, evaluator capacity, known dependence, available
outcome references, latency, privacy, and cost. Their own performance would be
measured against direct-review and simpler assisted baselines. The system would
learn which kinds of decomposition and challenge help, where they merely add
persuasion, and when the correct action is to abstain.

White-box methods would enter as competing instruments rather than privileged
windows into the model. Predictive and causal hypotheses would be challenged
across methods, checkpoints, data shifts, and behavioral controls. Monitor and
steering policies would be versioned, qualified, observed, rolled back, and
retired like other model changes. Unexplained computation and construct
uncertainty would remain visible.

At the frontier, the evidence system would continuously test its own trusted
base. It would ask whether evaluators share hidden dependencies, whether
selection pressure changes what the model reveals, whether reviewers are being
persuaded rather than informed, whether the evidence schema omits the decisive
property, and whether the governance burden itself is causing bypass. It would
generate countercases and preserve failures without allowing the learner to
rewrite protected histories or promote itself.

That mature state is a research target. The present repository does not
demonstrate a generally reliable scalable-oversight system, complete model
interpretability, evaluator independence, or a natural-work advantage for the
full claim ledger. Those are argument-exit obligations, not implied results.

## The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is that evidence machinery can produce epistemic
theater. A claim receives an identifier, vector, transition, reviewer,
dependency graph, and status panel. The process looks rigorous even when the
construct is wrong and every participant shares the same blind spot. Worse,
the structure can make a weak result persuasive because readers mistake
record completeness for truth.

This objection applies with special force to AI-assisted oversight. A model
can generate both the proposal and its critique, supply plausible alternatives,
and write the transition record. The human sees a polished debate and a green
validator. Internal evidence adds another layer of apparent access: a feature
plot or causal intervention makes the system look understood even when the
label, method, and coverage are fragile.

The architecture cannot eliminate this risk. Its answer is deliberately
limited. Record shape is not evidence truth. Roles are not independence.
Votes are not outcomes. Interventions are not completeness. Review does not
grant authority. Every layer preserves a route to no change, downgrade,
abstention, or refusal. The strongest baseline remains visible, and the richer
system must demonstrate decision value rather than assume it.

The machinery should be removed where it does not change conclusions. Low-risk
claims can use light records. Transparent artifacts can receive direct review.
Behavioral evidence can beat white-box analysis. A fixed review policy can beat
adaptive orchestration. The evidence system earns its complexity only through
better calibration, challenge, correction, and recovery on natural work.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The chapter's conclusion should narrow if a simpler append-only claim record
matches the full system on calibration, false promotion, challenge success,
negative-result retention, revision accuracy, and recovery cost. It should
narrow if direct expert review matches delegated protocols after equal access,
time, task difficulty, and outcome auditing. It should narrow if white-box
methods add no decision-relevant information beyond strong behavioral
baselines after compute, analyst effort, privacy, maintenance, and collateral
effects are counted.

The conclusion should strengthen only through matched natural correction
streams. Those streams need prospectively frozen claims and workloads,
complete outcome denominators, strong simple baselines, materially separated
evaluators, hard negative and positive controls, real model and task changes,
adversarial attempts to exploit review, and independently checked outcomes.
They must measure not only accuracy but false promotion, false quarantine,
coverage, selective risk, reviewer burden, latency, privacy, cost, residual
age, rollback, and recovery.

White-box promotion needs an additional burden: multiple method families,
construct alternatives, held-out behavioral prediction, necessity and
sufficiency distinctions, specificity and side-effect checks, checkpoint and
distribution stability, method disagreement, and a strong behavioral-only
baseline. A bounded gain must survive without becoming a claim of whole-model
understanding or safety.

Failure can also change the conclusion. If structured evidence records
systematically increase confidence without improving correctness, if review
protocols amplify persuasion or hide correlated error, or if the overhead
drives consequential work into unrecorded channels, the stack should simplify
or reject those mechanisms.

## What This Establishes

Evidence States owns how a claim's support may change. Scalable Oversight owns
the protocol by which limited evaluators, assistants, critics, auditors, and
escalation owners contribute bounded review. White-Box Evidence owns the
maximum inference that may survive from internal-state observation and
intervention. Adversarial Evaluation remains the broader owner for behavioral
and training-time observation integrity. These responsibilities interact, but
none inherits another's evidence or authority.

The practical rule is to keep the inference smaller than the artifact until a
claim-specific transition earns more. A passing test is not a method verdict.
A citation is not local reproduction. A proof is not runtime truth. A long
debate is not independent review. A human approval is not meaningful control
by default. An activation is not a concept. A causal intervention is not a
complete mechanism. A support transition is not permission to deploy or
publish.

For the incoming paper, the book can now say something precise. One example
may pass. One implementation subclaim may receive bounded support after exact
review. The broader method can remain untested. The oversight protocol can
record whether it found a real defect and what dependencies remain. The
internal observation can remain predictive, causal-bounded, unstable, or
rejected without forcing a universal verdict. Every conclusion retains the
evidence that produced it and the conditions that would expire it.

This discipline still depends on people. Someone chooses the claim, interprets
the request, defines the construct, sets the evidence threshold, and decides
whether a residual is acceptable. Those people can be overloaded, persuaded,
or mistaken. The next chapter moves into that human boundary: how an ambiguous

preserved under limited attention, and how communication itself becomes an
